activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Cortisol is a hormone made by the adrenal glands that rises during stress; when stress lasts a long time, cortisol can stay high.
story:
Dinner was chicken and rice, and Ms. Holloway from next door had brought over a casserole dish because she wanted her pan back and stayed to eat. She also wanted Aaron on her library quiz team, which was the third time she'd asked this month.

"I'll think about it," Aaron said, which was what he'd said the other two times.

"You look tired," his dad said.

Aaron pushed rice around his plate. "The doctor says I'm fine. She said the tiredness is probably from being stressed so long." He repeated it the way the doctor had said it to him. "Cortisol is a hormone made by the adrenal glands that rises during stress. When stress lasts a long time, cortisol can stay high." That was the whole explanation. No infection, no low iron, just chemistry that had been running hot for weeks.

"So it's not like a valve that opens and closes," his dad said. "More like a tap somebody left on."

"I guess." Aaron didn't want to guess. He wanted to know, and the doctor hadn't tested anything. So he decided to run his own test. If long stress kept cortisol high, and high cortisol made him feel run down, then cutting the stress should change something. He could measure that. Every day after school he'd rate his energy from one to ten in his notebook.

Ms. Holloway leaned forward. "You take on a great deal, Aaron. Basketball, jazz band, that robotics thing with Hafsa."

"Hafsa and Hallie both quit robotics," Aaron said. "They said they were setting boundaries. That's the word Hallie used. She said no to Tuesdays and Thursdays and her anxiety got better."

"Sounds like coping to me," Ms. Holloway said. "You could speculate all night about which activity is draining you, or you could find out."

He found out. He skipped jazz band for two weeks, just Tuesdays, and told Mr. Delaney it wasn't forever, only an experiment. His energy numbers climbed from threes to sixes. When he went back the following Tuesday, the number dropped to four. Basketball, dropped from the schedule the week after, made no difference at all; his numbers stayed at six.

At the next dinner, the notebook lay open beside his plate, graphs penciled in the margins. "It's jazz band," he told his dad. "Not the practicing. The performing."

"So what's the plan?"

"Bounditions," Aaron said, and Ms. Holloway laughed so hard she nearly knocked over her water.

"Boundaries," she corrected.

"Right." He tore off a corner of napkin and wrote it down. "Tuesdays only, and I'm telling Mr. Delaney tomorrow. And Ms. Holloway, if the quiz team meets on Thursdays, I'm in."

She raised her glass of water toward him. "Thursday it is."

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Fractures of the radius near the wrist are the most common fractures seen in children, and they usually happen from falling onto an outstretched hand.
story:
Emilia sat on the bench at the edge of the soccer field, her left arm in a bright green cast that ended just below her elbow. Mr. Ma had put her in charge of the stopwatch, since she couldn't play, and she was learning that watching a game from the sidelines showed you things you never noticed while running. For one thing, players fell constantly, and almost every single one of them threw a hand out to catch the fall.

She started keeping a second column on her clipboard, next to the sprint times. Tally marks for every tumble. Nearly all the falls ended the same way: palms slapping the grass, wrists bending back. It made her wonder. Her own fracture, the doctor had said, was of the radius, the bone on the thumb side of the forearm, right near the wrist, and it had happened exactly that way, when she'd pitched off her scooter and landed on an outstretched hand. The doctor had also mentioned that this was the most common fracture seen in children. Emilia looked at her tally marks, then at the green cast on her arm. Could she infer a rule from all this? It seemed like kids' wrists and the ground had some kind of standing appointment.

During the water break she found her classmate Jay, who was attempting a skateboard trick on the paved path beside the field, even though Mr. Ma had told him twice to knock it off. "Try to land on your forearm and slide," she said. "Not your hand. Trust me."

"That's radical advice from someone on a bench," Jay said, but he nodded.

She explained what she had figured out, pointing at her clipboard. "Radius, near the wrist. Most common fracture in kids. And you know how it happens? Falling onto an outstretched hand. Everybody does it. Watch." She nodded toward the field, where a midfielder had just gone down, hand out, wrist snapping back. Tally mark.

Jay attempted his kickflip anyway. He got most of the rotation, landed crooked, and pitched forward, and Emilia's stomach dropped as she watched both his hands shoot out in front of him like they belonged to somebody else. He sat on the pavement cradling his right wrist, which was already puffing up. An hour later he was in the emergency room, and the next morning he showed up at school with a sore, swollen wrist wrapped in a blue cast that ended just below the elbow.

"Radius, near the wrist," he said grimly, holding it up. "Falling on an outstretched hand, just like you said. You should charge money for that advice."

"Consider it free," Emilia said, "no warranty included." She was still laughing when the office aide came to find her, holding a note from her doctor. Her bone had healed ahead of schedule, and the cast could come off that very afternoon. She looked at Jay's fresh blue plaster, and then at her own green one, and held out her arm to admire it one last time.

"Enjoy the bench," Jay said. "I'll be keeping your tally marks warm."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: At a Passover Seder, the Jewish meal retelling the Exodus from Egypt, the youngest able child traditionally asks the Four Questions.
story:
Antoine stood in the doorway of the synagogue's social hall with a box of grape juice bottles balanced against his hip, wondering which table belonged to his aunt and uncle. The room smelled of chicken soup and candles. It was his first Seder without his grandmother, who had always hosted it in her cramped kitchen, and everything here felt too big and too bright.

He found his family near the window. His little cousin Zoe sat with a wrinkled paper in front of her, moving her lips without sound. Zoe was seven, the youngest kid at the table, and she had been practicing the Four Questions all week. Antoine knew because he had heard her through the wall of their shared hotel room, whispering the same Hebrew words over and over until he could almost recite them himself.

"Antoine," she whispered, grabbing his sleeve as he sat down. "What if I mess up?"

"You won't."

"But what if I freeze? In front of everybody?"

He looked around the hall. Forty people, maybe more. The rabbi was already pouring the first cup. Zoe's hands were shaking so badly the paper rattled against the tablecloth.

Antoine's mother lit the candles and said the blessing, and then the Seder began to move through its order, plate by plate, cup by cup. Zoe kept glancing at the paper, folding one corner, then another, until it looked as brittle as an old leaf. Antoine watched her and began to formulate a plan. If she panicked, someone had to be ready.

So he tested an idea, quietly, on his knee. While the adults sang, he mouthed the first question under his breath, the words he had absorbed through the hotel wall without meaning to. He got through the first line, stumbled on the second, and tried again. Next to him, his uncle's friend Mr. Anderson, a broad man with a loud laugh, gave him a curious look.

"You practicing too?" Anderson asked.

"No. Just in case."

"In case of what?"

Antoine didn't answer. Zoe was staring at the paper like it might bite her.

When the moment came, when his uncle lifted the matzah and nodded at her, Zoe stood up. She opened her mouth. Nothing came out. The whole hall waited. Her eyes went white and wide, and her paper slipped from her fingers onto the floor.

Antoine stood up beside her.

He started the first question, half a step behind the melody but close enough. Zoe's head snapped toward him. He kept going, a little slower, and on the second line her voice crept in under his, then rose above it. By the third question he wasn't leading anymore. He sat down and let her carry it alone through the fourth, clear and strong, while Mr. Anderson thumped the table and half the hall hummed along.

When she finished, Zoe dropped into her chair, grinning. She picked her paper up off the floor and smoothed it flat.

"You knew it the whole time?" she whispered.

"Only from listening to you."

She stared at him. "You could have just told me you'd do that."

"You'd have worried about me instead."

At the end of the night, after the last cup and the last song, his uncle caught Antoine at the coat rack. "That was quick thinking," he said. "Your grandmother would have done the same thing." He pressed a piece of afikoman into Antoine's hand, wrapped in a napkin, still a little warm.

"Split it with Zoe," Antoine said.

From across the hall, Zoe was already waving the paper at him. "Next year," she called, "I'm teaching you the whole thing."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: PolitiFact, a US fact-checking website founded in 2007, rates claims on a scale it calls the Truth-O-Meter, from True to Pants on Fire.
story:
Edouard slammed his notebook onto the lab table so hard that the beaker of water wobbled. "The ad said the mayor cut the bus budget in half," he told Lea-Rose and Nael. "My grandpa believed it before the commercial even finished. He said he's voting for the other guy now."

"Maybe she did," Nael said, stacking petri dishes because Mr. Bighorn had assigned cleanup duty and nobody wanted to salvage a detention on a Friday.

"She didn't. I just know it." Edouard tapped his pencil. The problem was that knowing and proving were not the same thing, and Mr. Bighorn had spent the whole week driving that point home. Last Tuesday he had made them drop steel wool into two test tubes, one capped and one open, and asked which one rusted and why. Edouard had figured out that something invisible in the air had to be causing it, even though nobody could see the cause directly. "You can't see air," Mr. Bighorn had said. "So you test what it does."

Lea-Rose leaned over her phone. "My mom does this thing when an ad makes her mad. She looks it up on PolitiFact. It's a fact-checking website, and it's been around since 2007." She scrolled, then turned the screen so both boys could see. "Look, they rate claims on a scale."

Nael squinted. "They call it the Truth-O-Meter," he read off the page. "It goes from True all the way to Pants on Fire."

Edouard grabbed the phone. There it was, the bus budget claim, with a little cartoon meter pointing almost to the bottom of the scale. The website hadn't just said the mayor was innocent, either. It showed the actual budget numbers, year by year, from records anyone could request. The budget had barely moved. The ad had taken one small cut and blown it up. That was the hidden mechanism, like the invisible something rusting the steel wool. A claim could look solid on the surface and still be corroded underneath.

"So it's not just that Grandpa's wrong," Edouard said slowly. "It's that somebody built that ad on purpose to make him wrong." It seemed ironic that a thirty-second commercial could do more work than months of real governing, and that people trusted the commercial.

On Monday, Edouard printed the fact check and brought it to his grandfather's apartment. He didn't lecture. He just set the pages on the kitchen table beside the coffee mug and said, "Look at the meter, Grandpa. Almost Pants on Fire."

His grandfather put on his glasses, read for a long time, and finally looked up. "Well," he said, "I still don't like her roads policy. But at least now I'm angry about a real thing."

"That's all I wanted," Edouard said, and slid the sugar bowl across the table.

activity: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
knowledge_domain: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
fact: With regular use, the brain adapts to nicotine, so a person needs more of it to feel the same effect; this is called tolerance.
story:
Samantha leaned over the sink in the second-floor bathroom and held her note cards at arm's length, because the fluorescent light made the ink look like it was floating. Tomorrow she had to explain, in four minutes, how nicotine hooks the brain, and right now her cards said things like "reward pathway = dopamine?" with a question mark she'd added at lunch.

"You're hiding in here again," said Courtney, coming in with her gym bag. "Mr. Watanabe said he'd allocate five minutes at the end of class for anyone who wants to practice."

"Four minutes. He said four, and I need all of them." Samantha set the cards down on the sink's edge, where a drip from the tap threatened the bottom one. Courtney noticed and slid a folded paper towel under them without saying anything about it.

"Okay, start over," Courtney said, and perched on the radiator by the window, which rattled when the wind came through the arid gap where the frame didn't quite meet the wall.

Samantha took a breath and began. "So nicotine gets into the brain and tricks the reward pathway, the same system that makes food taste good and makes you want to see your friends again. It floods it. The brain doesn't like being flooded." She stopped, staring at her cards. "And then... this is where it falls apart. My uncle stopped smoking three times. The last time he went from half a pack to a whole pack and I never understood why he didn't just stay at half."

Courtney's older sister vaped for a year before quitting, so Courtney leaned forward. "He needed more to feel the same thing?"

Samantha froze. She heard the pharmacist's voice from the counter where she'd stood with her uncle in March, him picking up patches, her waiting. The pharmacist had said, as she rang up the box, "With regular use the brain adapts to nicotine, so a person needs more of it to feel the same effect. That's called tolerance." Her uncle had nodded like he already knew, which maybe he did, in his own way, and Samantha had mostly been reading the candy display. But the line had stuck.

"That's it," she said now, scribbling on the back of a card. "The brain adapts. An adaptation, like the whole system recalibrates around the nicotine, so the old amount stops working. He wasn't choosing to smoke more. His brain was demanding it." She looked up. "That's the trap part. That's why quitting is hard, and that's the middle of my whole talk."

"Say the whole middle section to me," Courtney said, hopping off the radiator. "I'll time it."

Samantha squared the cards, tapped them once on the porcelain, and started talking to the mirror.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: Repeating an experiment several times helps show whether a result is real or just happened by chance.
story:
Every strawberry that had ripened in Rachel's garden had a neat bite taken out of it, always overnight, always from the side facing the fence. She crouched by the bed and turned a half-eaten berry in her fingers while Lilith peered over her shoulder. "My mom says it's birds," Lilith said. "Rohan says it's rabbits. He's so sure." Rachel wasn't sure of anything yet. She had a guess, though, that something was coming through the gap under the fence, and a guess, she figured, was only worth anything if you could test it. "That's called a hypothesis," she said. "A guess you can check."

She set up her test at dusk. Six ripe berries, three placed near the gap and three by the patio, each one dusted with flour so that anything touching it would leave tracks. In the morning she found tiny three-toed prints on the patio berries and nothing at all by the fence. Rabbits were out. The flour marks were so faint, though, that she couldn't yet distinguish real tracks from scratches the wind might have made, so she repeated the whole thing the next night, and the night after that. Three mornings in a row, the same pattern.

Meanwhile Rohan had brought his toy cars to the garden wall and built a ramp from an old plank. His red car beat Lilith's blue car once, and he crowned it on the spot, holding it overhead like a trophy. "Fastest car, proven forever," he announced. Rachel frowned. "You ran it one time." They raced again and the blue car won, then won twice more, and Rohan's champion turned out to be counterfeit, a title from a single lucky roll down the plank. "You have to run it several times," Rachel said, "or you can't tell a real winner from one that just happened by chance." Rohan looked at his car like it had lied to him.

On the fourth morning Rachel hid behind the shed before dawn, wrapped in her jacket, and watched the strawberry bed through the network of bean vines climbing the trellis. The thief came at last, and it wasn't a bird or a rabbit. It was Lilith's little sister, in pajamas, carefully biting one berry from each plant and leaving the rest, the neat three-toed prints explained by the plastic dinosaur clutched in her fist, dragging through the flour as she reached.

Lilith went pale when Rachel told her. "She's been sneaking out at night? Mom will freak." They made a deal: the little sister would get two berries each evening, picked honestly, and Rachel would keep the flour tests going one more week to be certain the pattern held. It meant giving up her best berries every night, and it meant Lilith walking home stiff and quiet, but the next morning the fence gap stayed untouched, and the patio berries ripened whole.

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: Chicago's Engine Company 21 is widely credited with the first fire pole, installed in 1878 after a firefighter slid down a pole faster than others could take the stairs.
story:
Charlie had one goal for the zoo field trip: win Mr. Perera's mystery-object challenge. Every quarter he picked a student who solved it, and that student got to feed the seals. She had lost twice to Sam already, and today she intended to fix that.

The class followed Mr. Perera past the insect house, where Arya stopped to press her magnifying lens against a case of jewel beetles. "If the mystery is another beetle," Arya said, "I'm keeping the lens."

"No beetles today," said Mr. Perera. He led them to a brick building tucked between the reptile house and the aviary, where a shiny brass pole ran from a hole in the ceiling all the way to the floor. "This building is the old fire station that used to stand here, before the zoo grew around it. That is the original pole, from Chicago's Engine Company 21. The question is: why did firefighters use a pole instead of stairs? Guesses, everyone."

"To look cool," said Sam immediately.

"To slide down carrying a cat they rescued," someone offered.

Charlie frowned at the pole. She had guessed wrong once before, about a turtle shell, and the memory still stung. But her history teacher had mentioned fire stations last week, and something was trying to germinate in her memory, a small seed of a fact pushing up through everything else she'd crammed for the quiz. Something about 1878.

"Was it speed?" she said slowly. "Like, in 1878, a firefighter at Chicago's Engine Company 21 slid down a pole, and he got down faster than the others who took the stairs?"

Mr. Perera raised an eyebrow. "You're not guessing, are you. You're remembering."

"That's cheating," said Sam, grinning.

"It's called learning," said Arya. "Look it up."

"It's not cheating, and it might not be right," Charlie said. She pointed at the metal stairs spiraling up beside the pole. "We could test it. Somebody climbs the stairs and somebody slides. Time both."

"With what?" said Sam.

Arya held up her phone. "I've been timing the sea lion show for my sister. My timer is very consistent. Two seconds, every time I test it."

Mr. Perera checked that the coast was clear, then gave permission. Sam clumped up the stairs while Charlie gripped the pole, and Arya counted down. Charlie dropped, slid, and landed with a squawk that made a passing peacock answer. Arya called out the times, and the slide beat the stairs by seconds, again and again, trial after trial.

"So the pole stayed because one man in 1878 was faster sliding than the others were on the stairs," Charlie said. "And it spread from Engine Company 21 to stations everywhere."

"Feeding time," said Mr. Perera, holding out a bucket of fish, and the whole class groaned as Charlie took it and jogged toward the seals, grinning at Sam over her shoulder. "Tomorrow," Sam called after her, "I'm memorizing the entire reptile house."

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: The law of supply says that when the price of a good rises, sellers usually offer more of it, because making and selling it becomes more profitable.
story:
The chili crisp shelf at Hartley's Grocery was almost bare, and the one jar left had a bright new sticker on it. Ellie leaned close and squinted. Last month the same jar had been five dollars. Now it said nine. She snatched it up anyway, because the cooking contest was Saturday and she needed it for her noodles, but the price itched at her all the way down the aisle.

She passed the pharmacy counter, where a man was arguing that his prescription should have been ready an hour ago, and the itch turned into a thought. "Maika's bracelets," she said out loud. A woman pushing a cart gave her a look, but Ellie didn't care. Back in September, Maika had sold her woven bracelets at the fall fair for eight dollars each, and every single one had sold out by noon. Two weeks later, Jaycob was selling bracelets, and the girl down the street, and even a table of them at the farmers market. When lots of people wanted something and there wasn't much of it, the price shot up. And when the price shot up, more people started selling it, because at eight dollars a bracelet it was suddenly worth your Saturday. She could still see Maika counting her money, grinning, while Jaycob studied her knots and said, "I could make these."

By the pasta aisle, Ellie had a plan. More sellers showing up wasn't some accident, it was inevitable, like the bracelets proved. If the chili crisp price had jumped, then somewhere, someone was deciding to make more of it and get in on that nine dollars. She just had to find that someone before Saturday. She put the expensive jar back on the shelf to conserve her allowance, which felt very brave, and hurried toward Mr. Tang's house two blocks over, because Mr. Tang made his own chili crisp in giant batches every autumn and the whole street knew it.

"Sold out," Mr. Tang said at his door, holding up empty hands. "Everyone wants it since that video went around. But," and he paused, rubbing his chin, "my cousin wants some of that nine-dollar money too. He's making a batch Thursday. Me, I'm making double my usual."

Ellie nearly bounced off the porch steps. Double! Her idea had been right, and now it had proof. "Can I reserve two jars?" she asked. "For the contest. I'll pay whatever you usually charge, not the store price."

Mr. Tang laughed and told her five dollars a jar, the old price, because she'd helped him carry boxes in the summer. On Thursday, Ellie stood in his kitchen while he ladled glowing red chili crisp into jars, the smell so sharp her eyes watered. She counted out her ten dollars, hugged the warm jars to her chest, and raced home to practice her noodles.

At the contest on Saturday, three other kids had brought chili crisp dishes, and one of them leaned over Ellie's table and whispered, "Where did you even find it? The store was cleared out and the price was crazy."

"Mr. Tang," Ellie said, spooning a little more over her noodles, "and get there early next time. He made double."

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: Historians check a diary against other sources, such as letters, newspapers and government records, to test whether its details are accurate.
story:
Emma slid the microfilm reel into the reader, and the newspaper page from 1847 glowed green on the screen. Her project was due Friday: use a primary source to explain why people moved west in the 1800s. She had chosen the diary of a settler named Ruth Carver, kept in the library's glass case, and she had copied out three pages of it in her notebook.

"There," said Leen, pointing at Emma's transcription. "Ruth writes that a fever went through their wagon train on June the third and her sister almost died." Leen frowned at the newspaper. "But this paper from June the third says the trains at that crossing were delayed by flooding, and lists no sickness."

Ms. Haile, the librarian, wheeled a cart of document boxes past their table. "Something wrong?" Emma showed her the two dates, and Ms. Haile said only, "Historians check a diary against other sources, such as letters, newspapers and government records, to test whether its details are accurate," and kept pushing the cart.

Emma stared at the screen. She had assumed the diary was right because Ruth had been there. But maybe Ruth had written the entries later, from memory, and had gotten the date wrong. She formed a simple test: if the fever happened at that time, other sources should mention it somewhere nearby. She scrolled the newspaper forward, day by day, the pages flickering and the machine humming warm beside her elbow.

On June the tenth she found it: a notice that a party of emigrants had halted at the crossing, "several persons ill of fever." Emma then checked the government land records in the orange box Ms. Haile had left on the hold shelf. Ruth's family filed their claim two weeks later than the diary said they arrived. One date in the diary, Emma saw, was off by a week. The other details, the flooding and the sickness, matched. Ruth had not lied; she had just misplaced the date.

"So the diary is wrong and the paper is right?" said Aliyah, arriving with her backpack still on.

"Half wrong," Emma said. "The fever was real, just not when Ruth said." She wrote at the top of her notes: never trust one source alone, because an assumption is not the same as evidence. Then she copied the June the tenth notice onto her page and underlined the word "fever" twice. Aliyah leaned over her shoulder and read the sentence out loud, and Emma slid the notebook across the table so she could see the microfilm screen herself.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: On a care label, an empty triangle means any bleach may be used, while a triangle with a cross through it means the garment must not be bleached.
story:
Brody stood in the kitchen with three piles of clothes on the floor and a folded note from his mom, who had left for a two-day work trip. The note said, "You wanted to do your own laundry. Prove it." He had begged for this after she shrunk his favourite hoodie, but now the washing machine glinting in the corner looked less like freedom and more like a corporation of buttons waiting to laugh at him.

He sorted the way he thought made sense: darks, lights, and a suspicious middle pile he decided to dismiss entirely by shoving into the dark load. Then he spotted his striped shirt, the one with the mystery ketchup stain from lunch. The stripes were white and navy, so bleach seemed like the obvious move. He carried the bottle toward the machine, then hesitated. His mom once ruined a red sock situation by guessing, and guessing had not gone well. He checked the little tag inside the collar, where a triangle with a cross through it stared up at him. "What does that even mean?" he muttered.

He texted Gordon, whose reply came in three seconds: "idk, my dad handles that." Brynlee answered a minute later with a photo of a label from her own shirt. Hers had an empty triangle, no cross. "mine says the plain one means any bleach is fine," she wrote. Brody laid both facts side by side in his head. If an empty triangle meant any bleach may be used, then the crossed-out triangle on his striped shirt meant the opposite: it must not be bleached. It was like the tag was warning him in code, and he had almost cracked the code the wrong way. He put the bleach back under the sink and ran the shirt through with ordinary detergent instead, setting the machine by matching the dial to the words on his mom's note.

While the wash churned, Ms. Ferreira, the neighbour whose kitchen window faced his, knocked on the screen door. "Your machine sounds like it's doing gymnastics," she said. Brody invited her in, and she watched him move the load to the dryer with an air of amused inspection. "I once bleached a whole load of my husband's socks," she offered. "Every one came out yellow." "Yellow?" Brody said. "That's not even a bleach colour." "Exactly," she said. "Respect the tags."

When the dryer buzzed, he folded everything on the counter, wobbling through his first fitted-sheet attempt, which looked like a fabric potato. But the striped shirt came out clean, stripes intact, ketchup gone. He laid the shirt on top of the stack and took a photo for his mom, then set it as his lock screen. Then he started the second load.

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: Two climate graphs can only be compared by bar height if their rainfall axes use the same scale; otherwise a short bar may stand for more rain.
story:
The library was closed on one side for construction, because the city had decided to renovate the whole building at once, so everyone crammed into the small reading room near the front desk. Louis spread out two climate graphs on the table, one for a desert city and one for a rainforest city, plus the assignment sheet that read: compare rainfall and temperature.

"Easy," said Shea, sliding into the chair across from him. "The rainforest bars are taller, so it rains more there. Done. Can we go get snacks?"

Maddie leaned over the paper with the acute concentration she saved for proving Shea wrong. "Wait. Look at this one. The desert bars go up to twenty." She tapped the paper. "But the rainforest bars stop around fifteen. So the desert gets more rain? That can't be right. It's a desert."

"Bars are bars," Shea said. "Taller is wetter. Fifteen loses to twenty. That's just math."

"That's not math, that's a staring contest," Maddie said. She folded her arms. "Rainforests are famously soaked. There's a reason nobody brings a beach towel to the desert."

Louis pulled the graphs toward himself. Something about the argument bothered him, like an itch he couldn't reach. The bars were drawn as if they were competing, but bars were only pictures, and pictures could trick you. He stared at the numbers running up the left side of each graph, the rainfall axis, and there it was.

"Shea, read the numbers on the side of the desert graph."

Shea squinted. "Zero, five, ten, fifteen, twenty. Millimeters, it says."

"Now the rainforest one."

"Zero, fifty, one hundred." Shea stopped. His mouth stayed open a moment. "Oh no."

"Each little line on the rainforest graph is fifty millimeters," Louis said. "On the desert one it's five. So that short bar that stops around fifteen? That's actually three hundred millimeters of rain in one month."

Maddie clapped once, loud enough that the librarian looked over and shushed them, which was unfair, since Maddie considered a single clap to be very quiet. "So the taller bars in the desert graph are an illusion," she said. "The scale is squished. The little rainforest bars stand for way more rain."

"So when you compare them," Shea said slowly, like the words cost him something, "you can't just look at bar heights unless both graphs count by the same numbers."

"That," said Maddie, "was almost painful for you."

Louis was already flipping both graphs over to write on the back, where he could redraw the desert bars on the rainforest scale. On the new axis, the desert's proud tall bars shrank into stubby little teeth. Shea picked up a green marker and drew a tiny umbrella over the rainforest city, then a tiny sun with sunglasses over the desert, and under the desert sun he wrote, in careful letters, "still basically a toaster."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A checkable claim can be false; 'The Eiffel Tower is in Berlin' is a wrong factual claim, not an opinion.
story:
Jack pushed his pasta around the plate while his father read aloud from his phone. "Violet's uncle posted that the new bridge is going to collapse within a year," his father said. "That's his opinion, I suppose."

"That's not an opinion," Jack said. "It's a claim. You could go look at the bridge, or read the engineers' report, and find out if it's true or not."

His father raised an eyebrow. "And an opinion can't be checked?"

"Right. Like if Mohamed-Amine says the cafeteria pizza is disgusting. Nobody can test that. It's just how it tastes to him."

His little sister, still in her high chair, banged her spoon, and his mother said dinner was not a debate club. But Jack kept thinking about it, because tomorrow he and Mohamed-Amine had agreed to finish their geography project, and the project was a problem.

The problem was this. Mohamed-Amine had written, in big letters on their poster, "The Eiffel Tower is in Berlin." When Jack had told him that was wrong, Mohamed-Amine had shrugged and said, "It's my opinion." Mr. Campbell had already looked at the poster once and said they'd discuss it on Friday. If Mohamed-Amine wouldn't change it, their grade would sink, and Jack's mother had promised him a new bike if his project mark came back above a B.

So at lunch the next day, Jack tried an experiment. He borrowed Mr. Campbell's atlas from the shelf by the window, the one with the glossy photos, and laid it open on the table. "Show me where the Eiffel Tower is," he said.

Mohamed-Amine flipped to the index, ran his finger down the page, and stopped. The atlas placed the Eiffel Tower firmly in Paris, France. He stared at it for a long moment, then laughed. "Okay, okay. It's a wrong claim. Not an opinion. An opinion is like me saying Paris looks better in the rain."

"That's an opinion," Jack agreed. "Nobody can check it."

They fixed the poster together. Jack suggested they could even add a line explaining which parts of their project were facts and which were their own opinions about the landmarks, which Mohamed-Amine thought was clever, though he refused to let Jack exclude his drawing of the tower wearing sunglasses. "It's not trivial," he insisted. "It's the best part."

On Friday, Mr. Campbell read the poster twice, tapped the Eiffel Tower entry, and said, "Well done. This is the difference most adults still mix up."

At dinner that night, Jack's father put down his phone. "I texted Violet's uncle," he said. "Asked him for the engineers' report." He slid his phone across the table, and Jack leaned in to read the message glowing on the screen.

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: The climax is the turning point of a story, the moment of highest tension when the main conflict is decided one way or the other.
story:
Nathaniel slid his draft across the cafe table so Nash and Hargun could both see it. "Mr. Clarke-Williams said it's due tomorrow, and it has to have real dialogue punctuation and a climax."

"Your commas are all outside the quotation marks," Nash said, tapping the page with his straw. "Half of them, anyway."

"That's the easy part," Hargun said. "The commas go inside when the dialogue tag comes after. The hard part is the climax. I read your story twice, and I can't tell which scene it is."

Nathaniel frowned. His story was about a kid whose basement flooded and who had to figure out whether to tell his dad that the plumbing repair kit he'd bought with his birthday money was a fake. He pointed at the middle. "There. That's the biggest scene. The water's everywhere."

"No, it's the end," Nash said. "When he finally confesses."

They argued until the cashier came over with a plate of cinnamon toast nobody remembered ordering, set it down next to Nathaniel, and quietly refused payment. "You three look like you're solving world hunger," she said, and went back to the counter.

Nathaniel chewed slowly, thinking. The flood wasn't the turning point, he realized. The water rising was just the problem getting worse. Nothing was decided there. The moment everything tipped one way or the other was smaller and quieter, when the kid opened his mouth in front of his dad. That was the moment when the conflict got settled.

"I think I've got it," he said. "The climax is the turning point of the story, the moment of highest tension when the main conflict is decided one way or the other. It's not the loudest scene. It's the deciding scene."

Nash read the pages again, lips moving. "So when he confesses and finds out his dad already knew. Yeah. That's it."

"That means I have to move it later," Nathaniel said. "Right now it's on page three and the flood is on page five. The tension drops after."

"So cut the flood down," Hargun said, "and let the confession carry the ending."

Nathaniel borrowed a pen from the cashier, crossed out two whole paragraphs about water migrating across the basement floor toward the boxes of old photographs, and drew an arrow pushing the confession scene to the last page. He was afraid it might be vain to think he could fix a whole story with one arrow, but he drew it anyway, dark and certain.

"Read me the new last line," Nash said.

Nathaniel held the page up to the window light. "'I never bought the kit,' I said, and my dad just laughed."

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Dots on the iron symbol set the highest safe iron setting: one dot is low, about 110 degrees Celsius, two is medium, about 150, and three is high, about 200.
story:
Hazel stood in front of the washing machine with three hampers of clothes and forty minutes before her mother's car pulled out for the drama banquet. Ms. Mehta, the neighbour who had offered to supervise, tapped the machine's lid. "Sorting first," she said. "You don't want your white choir shirt swimming with that red costume vest." Hazel dumped everything onto the kitchen floor and made piles: darks, whites, and the strange in-between stack that seemed to contradict the whole system, a striped towel, a purple sock. She and Larissa had made an alliance last week to split banquet prep, Larissa handling the bake sale table while Hazel got their costumes clean, and Hazel had promised on the bus, hand raised, that she'd handle it.

The dark load went in first because the vest was the urgent thing. While the machine churned, Hazel read the detergent cup twice, measured, and poured, and then wiped up the blue spill before Ms. Mehta could see it. When the vest came out dripping, they moved to the dryer, and Hazel learned that the elastic waistband of her stage pants meant low heat, because high heat, Ms. Mehta said, could ruin the stretch. Hazel filed that away. The shirt, though, the slippery nylon one with the pearly buttons, looked wrinkled even after tumbling, and the banquet was in twenty minutes.

"Use the iron," Ms. Mehta said, sliding the board open against the kitchen wall. "Cotton setting, that's the hot one." Hazel cranked the dial to cotton, waited until the plate felt fierce when she held her hand above it, and pressed it to the sleeve. There was a faint slick sound, and when she lifted the iron, the fabric shone in a hard, glassy patch where the wrinkle used to be. She touched it. The shine stayed, cool and stiff under her thumb, like the ghost of the wrinkle.

"Umar did that to his dad's tie once," Larissa said over the phone, which Hazel had propped against the sugar jar. "He said it looked like plastic." Hazel turned the shirt over and checked the little white tag sewn into the seam. There was a picture of an iron, and under it, printed small, three dots. On her stage pants the tag showed an iron with one dot. On the cotton choir dress from the finished pile, an iron with two dots.

"Cotton has two dots," Hazel said slowly. "The dress is cotton. So two dots must be the setting for cotton, and this shirt has three dots, and I had it on cotton, so." She turned the iron's dial down and down until the little indicator pointed to the lowest mark, the one-dot territory, which Ms. Mehta said was around 110 degrees Celsius. Two dots, she said, was medium, about 150, and three dots was high, about 200. Hazel hadn't asked what the shirt's three dots meant, and now the shiny sleeve did the explaining. She remembered choosing cotton because it sounded like the strongest setting, the grown-up setting, and she hadn't looked at the tag at all.

She wet a corner of the cotton dress and tested the low setting on a hidden hem of the pants first, then the shirt's collar, easing the iron along the seam. The collar flattened without shining. The sleeves were next, and the glassy patch on the left sleeve stayed, but Hazel flipped the cuff over it and pressed the buttons flat and decided the shine would have to be a story for the banquet table. Ten minutes left. She folded the vest along its shoulders, rolled the elastic-waist pants instead of creasing them, and hung the shirt on the back of a kitchen chair where the steam could finish the last stubborn pleat.

Ms. Mehta looked at the sleeve patch and then at Hazel, as if deciding whether to say something, and then just checked the time. "Your mother's in the driveway," she said. Hazel grabbed the hangers, phone still warm in her pocket, and the kitchen door swung shut behind her as she called, "Larissa, I'm coming, and I ironed something without burning the whole shirt."

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: Average speed equals distance travelled divided by the time taken.
story:
Isla crouched beside the ramp in the Motion Gallery, holding her marble the way a bowler holds a ball. Walid had beaten her three races in a row, and his marble wasn't even the shiny one. "Best of five," he said, and his marble zipped down the track and rolled to the line first again.

"It's not fair," Isla said. "My marble goes slow at the top and fast at the end. Yours is steady the whole way. How do we even compare them?" Arthur, who was timing with the museum's stopwatch at the bottom of the ramp, shrugged. "Yours lost. That's the comparison." But Isla couldn't resign herself to that. A slow start and a strong finish felt different from a boring roll all the way through, and she wanted to prove it with numbers, not just argue about it.

She borrowed a tape measure from the activities desk and crouched at the bottom of the ramp. She measured the whole track, then called out marks every metre along the floor. Arthur timed each race, but now he called the times at each mark as the marbles passed. Isla wrote everything in her notebook: one metre at four seconds, two metres at six, three at seven. Then she flipped to a clean page and drew two axes, distance going up and time going across, because she'd seen a graph like that on the wall by the pendulum exhibit.

Her points made a line that bent upward, steeper and steeper. "Steeper means faster," she said, mostly to herself, and Walid leaned over to see. Then she did the thing that made it click. She took her marble's total distance and divided it by the total time it took, and did the same for Walid's. "The whole race, we're almost the same," she said. "Six metres in ten seconds, six metres in nine and a half. But look at the graph. Mine ends faster than it starts. Yours never changes." Arthur frowned at his stopwatch. "So there's a number for the whole trip?" Isla nodded. "Average speed," she said. "Distance travelled divided by the time taken." Walid's marble had won every race, but by less each time.

Ms. Menon, the guide who had been restocking the activity table, stopped behind them and looked at Isla's page. "Would you like to try the long ramp downstairs? It's twice as far." Isla grinned and stood up. Then Walid held out his marble, and Isla saw it was dented on one side, the dent she'd noticed weeks ago and never mentioned. A small wave of guilt passed through her, because a dent seemed like nothing, a trivial little flaw, until it wasn't. "Race you," she said, and they ran for the stairs.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: Green or yellow mucus comes from immune cells and an enzyme they release, so its color alone does not show whether an infection is caused by bacteria or a virus.
story:
Amelia was on day four of the flu, camped on the living room couch with a box of tissues, a mug of honey tea, and a blanket her dad had tucked around her twice before leaving for his workshop downstairs. He was an artisan who carved wooden bowls, and she could hear the sander humming through the floor. Her symptoms had started to deteriorate on day two, when the cough deepened and her fever climbed, but this morning the fever was gone and she only felt stuffed up and tired.

Her phone buzzed. It was Ranveer, from science class. "Amelia. HELP. My nose just produced something GREEN. Like actually green. My mom says that means bacteria and I need medicine from the doctor. Is that true? You had this flu before me."

Amelia looked over at her own tissue pile. Hers had turned a distinct yellowish green yesterday, and today they were almost back to pale. She was clearly getting better, not worse. If green meant bacteria, shouldn't she be feeling terrible? Something did not add up, and she wanted to know what.

"Give me a minute," she typed, then waved her mom over and asked about the green tissues. Her mom scrolled on her phone, frowning, and read a line from the pharmacy's information page. Then she turned the screen so Amelia could see it herself. "It says here the color comes from immune cells," her mom said, "and from an enzyme they release."

Amelia read the whole paragraph twice. So the green stuff was her own immune cells, showing up to do their job, plus an enzyme they released while doing it. That meant green was a sign her body was fighting, not a sign of which germ it was fighting. Nowhere did it say the color could tell bacteria from a virus. She tested the idea against her own case: green tissues, no fever, improving by the hour. If green automatically meant bacteria, she would not be on the mend without any medicine at all.

She texted Ranveer back. "Relax. Green just means immune cells and an enzyme they release. The color alone can't tell you if it's bacteria or a virus. I had green for two days and I'm almost fine now. Rest, drink stuff, and if you get worse or it goes on forever, then your mom takes you in." She set the phone down, blew her nose one more time, and watched the tissue. Pale green. Still improving. Downstairs, the sander went quiet, and her dad's footsteps started up the stairs, carrying a small carved bowl he'd made to hold her tea bag.

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: The word diaspora comes from a Greek word meaning scattering, and it describes a people living spread out far from the homeland of their ancestors.
story:
The group chat lit up at 9:04 p.m., and Andrew read it upside down on his phone while pretending to finish his essay.

Carmen: FESTIVAL TABLE IS OURS. Saturday, 10 a.m. Who's in?
Eugene: in. my mom says she'll lend the folding table
Andrew: in. what's the banner say tho

Carmen posted a photo of the banner she had painted, deep blue with gold letters: ARMENIAN DIASPORA OF MILLBROOK. Andrew stared at it. He knew Carmen's family was Armenian the way he knew Eugene's dad was from Ghana, but he had never seen the word on the banner before.

Andrew: what does diaspora mean
Eugene: no idea. sounds like a plant
Carmen: honestly?? I put it on the banner because my grandma's friend uses it. I think it's important. Don't tell anyone I don't know what my own banner says.

Andrew typed "lol" and then deleted it, because Carmen rarely asked for help, and when she did she meant it. He had an idea, though. He planned to test it the next day, like Mr. Gauthier had shown them in science: when you can't see the cause of something, gather evidence and look for the pattern.

At school he found Mr. Gauthier hauling boxes of dodgeballs to the gym. "Quick question," Andrew said. "Do you have a dictionary in your classroom?"

"The big one on the shelf, behind the volcano model," Mr. Gauthier said, and kept walking.

The dictionary was heavy enough that Andrew had to rest it on two desks. He ran his finger down the column and found it. Diaspora. From a Greek word meaning scattering. It described a people living spread out far from the homeland of their ancestors. He copied it onto his hand with a pen because his notebook was in his locker and the bell was in four minutes.

Saturday morning, Carmen's table stood under a maple tree, the banner tacked above jars of dried apricots and a photo of her great-grandparents' village. A woman stopped, read the banner, and frowned at it.

"That's a lovely word," she said. "What does it mean, exactly?"

Carmen opened her mouth. Eugene looked at his shoes.

"It means scattering," Andrew said, wiping chalk dust off his palm. "It comes from a Greek word. It's when a people live spread out, far from the homeland of their ancestors."

The woman nodded slowly. "Like my mother's people," she said, and pointed to another table across the field, where a family was hanging flags. "We're the Hmong community table. I suppose we're one too." She bought two jars of apricots.

Carmen pulled Andrew behind the tree. "You went and looked it up."

"Somebody had to. Also, my mom signed me up for Saturday Turkish classes at the community foundation, so if I'm going to spend my weekends learning words anyway." He shrugged. "It seemed feasible to just find this one."

"That's not the same as feasible."

"It worked, didn't it?"

Eugene leaned around the trunk. "There's a line at the table and they're all asking about the banner now."

Carmen straightened the jars, took a breath, and walked back to the front of her own table. "Diaspora," she said to the next person in line, "comes from a Greek word. It means scattering."

activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
knowledge_domain: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
fact: The pH scale was introduced in 1909 by Danish chemist Søren Sørensen, who worked at the Carlsberg Laboratory in Copenhagen.
story:
Grandpa's kitchen smelled like vinegar and something he refused to identify, which was how the whole argument started. He had set out six unlabeled jars on the counter and a stack of small paper strips that turned colors when you dipped them.

"You're telling me you can identify a mystery liquid with paper," said Graeme, who had come along because Ariana's grandpa let them negotiate extra cookies before dinner.

"I'm telling you nothing," Grandpa said. "Ariana's telling you."

Ariana dipped a strip into the first jar. It turned red. She wrote "acid" on her chart, then tried the second jar, where the strip went blue. "Base," she said. "So the vinegar's in here somewhere, and the baking soda water, and I'm guessing the pickle brine." She held up a jar of something amber. "This one's barely changing color, so it's close to neutral. Could be the tea."

Graeme leaned over the chart. "You realize this proves nothing. You don't know which jar is which. You could be making it all up."

"I could write the answers on slips and put them in the jars," Ariana said. "Anonymous answers. You check them after I guess."

Grandpa approved of this so much he let them have the cookies early.

Leila arrived halfway through, drawn by the smell and the shouting. "My cousin says the pH scale was invented by an American," she announced. "He says it was some guy in a lab in Boston."

"It was not," Graeme said, though he had no idea. Neither did Ariana, and neither did Grandpa, who said only that he was not a chemist, he was a retired postal worker with a science kit.

The argument might have gone on all afternoon except that Ariana noticed the poster that came folded inside the kit. It showed the pH scale from zero to fourteen with a picture of a serious man with a mustache. She flattened it on the table.

"'The pH scale was introduced in 1909 by Danish chemist Søren Sørensen, who worked at the Carlsberg Laboratory in Copenhagen,'" she read.

"Carlsberg," said Grandpa. "That's a beer."

"So your cousin is wrong twice," Ariana told Leila. "It was a Dane, and it was at a beer lab, not Boston."

Leila took a photo of the poster for evidence, then claimed a monopoly on the last cookie as a settlement fee. Graeme objected. Ariana dipped one more strip, watched it turn a perfect purple, and slid the cookie jar out of everyone's reach.

"Neutral," she said. "Like me."

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: Section 33 of the Canadian Charter, the notwithstanding clause, lets Parliament or a provincial legislature override certain rights for up to five years, and the override can be renewed.
story:
Zoey pressed her interview sheet against the folding table outside the gym doors, where the polling station had taken over the whole basketball court. Mr. Nowak, their social studies teacher, had given the class one job: read a right from the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, explain it in their own words to a voter, and get a signature. "The election is your classroom today," he had said, and Zoey had been repeating that to herself all morning like a lucky coin.

"Which right did you pick?" London asked, bouncing on her toes beside the coat rack that served as the classroom's coat rack, since there was no classroom.

"Section 2, freedom of expression," Zoey said. "But I want to get it exactly right, because last weekend I got something wrong and it still bugs me."

Flashback: her grandmother's kitchen on Sunday, the radio going, her uncle insisting that a province could just cancel a right whenever it wanted. Zoey, wanting to sound sophisticated, had declared that once a right was overridden, it was gone forever, like a phone dropped in the lake. Her cousin had laughed and pulled up the actual text. Section 33, the notwithstanding clause. Parliament or a provincial legislature could override certain rights, but only for up to five years, and then the override could be renewed. Five years, then five more. Not forever, but not never, either. Zoey had gone quiet, ears hot, and copied the whole thing into her notebook so it could never sneak away from her again.

Back at the polling station, Mackenzie waved from the voter lineup. "Mr. Nowak says the first voter to sign your sheet gets a bonus point! The line's moving!"

"I have a theory," Zoey said, hurrying over. "I think most people here don't know their rights cold. Rights aren't something you inherit, like your grandmother's ring or your eye color. You have to actually read them." She decided to test it. She would explain freedom of expression to three separate voters, in her own words, and count how many already knew what Section 2 covered.

The first voter, a woman with a canvas tote full of library books, signed immediately and said, "Numbered clauses and everything. You've done your homework." The second, a man in a muddy work jacket, shrugged and admitted he mostly knew "the big ones, the ones on the news." The third was her own mother, who had volunteered as a poll worker and was stacking ballots at a table near the far wall.

"Mom. Freedom of expression. Say what you think, believe what you believe, and the government can't gag you," Zoey recited, "unless somebody invokes Section 33, which they can only do for up to five years at a time, and then they can renew it if they still want the override."

Her mother set down the ballot stack. "When did you become a constitutional lawyer?"

"When I got something wrong at Grandma's and promised never again," Zoey said, holding out the pen. "Sign here."

Her mother signed, and Mr. Nowak, passing by with a clipboard, glanced at the sheet and raised both eyebrows. "Three for three," he said. "Even the rodent control guy at the door said you sounded like you'd argued it in court."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: In March 1933, Joseph Goebbels became head of Nazi Germany's new Reich Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda.
story:
Riley needed a topic for Ms. Rowe's media project by Friday, and the only thing she knew for sure was that every ad she looked at seemed to be playing a trick on her. She spread three magazine pages across the library table: one for a sneaker worn by a famous singer, one for a soda that claimed "everyone is switching," and one for a phone that called its rival "pathetic."

"Those are three different tricks," said Emeric, dropping into the chair beside her. "The singer one is a celebrity testimonial. The soda one is bandwagon. And pathetic is a loaded word. My brother learned that in high school."

"You're making that up," Riley said, but she wrote all three phrases down anyway. Then she frowned at her notebook. "But who figured this stuff out? Somebody had to study it first."

Layla slid a book across the table toward her. It was about World War II, thick and full of posters. Riley flipped it open and stopped at a photograph of a poster with a crowd of marching figures and one bold line underneath: A whole people follows its leader. She recognized the trick instantly, the same one as the soda ad. Farther down the page, another poster called enemies "parasites" and promised to "eliminate" them, and the word hit her hard, the way "pathetic" was meant to, only worse.

"Look at this," Riley said. "They used every trick on people, not to sell soda but to make them hate." She read the caption twice, tracing it with her finger. "It says in March 1933, Joseph Goebbels became head of Nazi Germany's new Reich Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda. A whole government ministry just for this."

"So the tricks aren't new," Layla said quietly.

Riley tested the idea right there. She went down the page of posters, tapping each one. Bandwagon, the marching crowd. Loaded words, parasites. Then a poster of a smiling actress holding a radio, and Riley laughed without any humor in it. "Even a celebrity testimonial. It's all here, from almost a hundred years ago." She copied the caption into her notebook, then wrote her project title at the top of a fresh page: Same Tricks, Different Century.

Ms. Rowe passed by and paused at the little display of ads and posters they had laid out side by side.

"You found the through-line," Ms. Rowe said.

"That's the word," Riley told her. "I thought people back then must have been naive to fall for it. Then I caught myself wanting those sneakers because a singer wears them. The honey's still nectar, even when you watch the bees making it." She lined up the magazine pages next to the book, sneaker ad beside marching crowd, and tapped them both. "I want to stand up in class and hold these two together."

activity: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense
knowledge_domain: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense
fact: Spanish speakers often talk about plans with "ir a" plus an infinitive, as in "Voy a estudiar," meaning "I am going to study."
story:
The assignment on the board read "Mis planes para el ano proximo," five sentences, future tense, due at the end of the period. Naomi sat at the diagonal corner table in the library, farthest from Mr. Harper's desk, with her textbook open to the chapter on the future. The chapter gave one rule: add endings to the verb. "Estudiare," she wrote, then stopped. It looked wrong, like a word in no language at all.

Neriah slid into the chair across from her. "Mine's done. Five sentences, all with the endings." She turned her paper so Naomi could see it. Every verb carried the same little tail.

"Where'd you learn that?" Naomi asked.

"Same chapter you're on. Page ninety-two." Neriah tapped the book. "Just copy the pattern."

Naomi frowned at her paper. Last Sunday she had called her grandmother in Bogota to ask what she was doing next year, and her grandmother had said, "Voy a visitar a mi hermana." No ending on visitar. Naomi had assumed her grandmother had made a mistake, because grandmothers who talked fast made mistakes. But now she wasn't sure. Two rules couldn't both be right, or maybe they could, and only one of them was what people actually said.

"I'm going to test something," she said. She wrote five new sentences, all with "voy a" in front of a plain verb. "Voy a estudiar en la biblioteca. Voy a jugar baloncesto. Voy a visitar a mi abuela." Then she carried the paper to Mr. Harper's desk.

"Can you check these?" she asked.

He read them, and his eyebrows went up a little. "Where did you learn this?"

"My grandmother said 'voy a visitar.' I thought she messed it up, since the chapter never mentioned it. Does it mean the same thing?"

"'Voy a estudiar' means 'I am going to study,'" Mr. Harper said. "It's how Spanish speakers often talk about plans. 'Ir a' plus the infinitive. The chapter's endings aren't wrong, just less common for this."

Naomi went back to the table. She wanted to keep her first draft, the one with the endings, because she'd worked hardest on it and because Neriah had finished first. But a paragraph that nobody would actually say felt like a lie with good grammar. She crossed out the endings, one by one, eliminating each carefully built tail until only "voy a" and the plain verbs remained.

Neriah looked over. "You're changing your whole paper?"

"Yours isn't wrong," Naomi said. "Mine's just more right."

Neriah studied her own five sentences for a long moment, then grabbed her eraser. "Show me the first one again."

Together they rebuilt both papers, and when the bell rang, Neriah read her last line out loud: "Voy a viajar a Colombia con Naomi."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Two people can agree on every fact about an event and still interpret it differently because they value different things, such as fairness versus loyalty.
story:
The meeting of the robotics club started the way it always did, with Ms. Katz adjusting the projector and someone's elbow knocking over the bin of screws. But today nobody laughed, because everyone was waiting for the vote about Malcolm. Two weeks ago at the regional competition, their code had crashed because Stefano had stayed up all night fixing his little brother's wheelchair ramp instead of testing the robot. Malcolm had covered for him, telling the judges that the battery was faulty. The judges believed it. Malcolm had a reputation for honesty, which was exactly what made the lie work, and now half the club wanted him removed and the other half wanted him thanked.

Anais sat in the back with her notebook, trying to figure out why the club was tearing itself apart. She had listened to the arguments at lunch, in the hallway, even in the parking lot where Stefano's mom picked them up. The strange thing was that nobody disagreed about what had actually happened. Everyone agreed that Stefano had skipped testing, that Malcolm had lied, that the lie had won them second place, and that the judges would probably never find out. Those were the facts. She wrote them down in a column and stared at them, because if the facts were the same for everybody, then the fight had to be about something else, something she couldn't see directly. She had a theory, and she decided to test it the way she'd test a hypothesis in science: by controlling the variables.

She raised her hand before the shouting could start again. "Before we vote, let's do something. Everybody write down what happened, just the facts, no opinions. Then we compare."

Malcolm smirked at her from the front row. "You think we're too gullible to know the difference between a fact and a feeling?"

"I think we're too loud to check," Anais said, and Ms. Katz, who had wisely enrolled herself in the club only as a supervisor and refused to interfere in club decisions, nodded once and passed out sticky notes.

The club wrote. When they read the notes aloud, Anais felt a small electric thrill, the kind she got when a circuit suddenly worked. Every single note matched. Faulty battery, lie, wheelchair ramp, second place. Nobody argued over a single word of the facts. Then she asked the second question: "Now write whether Malcolm did right or wrong."

The room split exactly down the middle, and the sticky notes told her why. One side had written things like "he protected a teammate" and "Stefano's brother needed the ramp." The other side had written "he lied to judges" and "other teams played fair." It wasn't the event they were fighting about. It was what mattered most. She said it out loud, carefully, the way you'd handle a live wire: "We all agree on every fact. We just don't agree on what counts more. Half of us cares about fairness to the other teams, and half of us cares about loyalty to each other."

The room went quiet in a different way than before. A boy named Malcolm's friend, no, it was Malcolm himself, leaned back and rubbed his jaw. "So the vote isn't really about me," he said slowly. "It's about which one we think is bigger."

"Which is a vote we can still take," Stefano said, "but at least now we know what we're voting on." His voice was rough, and Anais remembered him at the competition, hands shaking, whispering "don't say anything" to Malcolm in the hallway. He'd been ashamed then. She wasn't sure he was ashamed now, or if that was even the right thing to feel, and she noticed she couldn't decide about herself either.

Ms. Katz collected the sticky notes, smoothed them into a stack, and pinned them to the corkboard next to the robot's wiring diagram, red opinions on one side, plain facts on the other. "You might want to look at this board before the next argument," she said. "Or before the next vote." Then she handed the marker to Anais, because the list of who would speak first was hers to write.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: A break statement stops a loop immediately, so a prime checker can quit as soon as it finds a single divisor.
story:
The computer lab at Camp Whitmore smelled like pine from the open windows and like burnt popcorn from the counselor's microwave down the hall. Oliver sat in front of a monitor with his program half finished, tapping the space bar while he thought. His dad had to commute forty minutes into the city every morning, and all week Oliver had imagined showing him something real at pickup on Saturday: a program that asked for a number and said whether it was prime.

Mr. Farah-Ali had given them only the bare outline. "Ask for a number," he had said that morning, walking between the rows of desks. "Then check it. The checking part is yours to figure out." Oliver had written a loop that tried every divisor from two up to the number itself, and a line that printed "not prime" whenever the remainder came out zero.

He typed 51 and hit enter. "Not prime" scrolled up the screen. Then again. Then again. He watched the column of identical words pile up, fifty of them, one for every divisor that failed before he found the one that worked. "It's having a breakdown," said Tatum, leaning over from the next seat. "It's fine, it's just dramatic." Oliver laughed, but he kept staring at the screen. The program wasn't wrong, exactly. It just didn't know when to stop talking.

He scrolled back through his loop and traced it with his finger on the glass. The rule he wanted was simple: the moment any single divisor worked, the answer was settled, prime or not, and everything after that was noise. He'd read the word "break" in the handout Mr. Farah-Ali had left on the front table, and he'd skipped it. Now he looked it up again. A break statement stops the loop immediately. He put one under his print line, so the loop would quit as soon as it found a single divisor, and ran the program again with 51.

"Not prime." Once. The screen sat quiet after that, like a person who had said what needed saying and closed their mouth. Oliver tried 97 next, and the loop ground all the way through without finding anything, and printed "prime." He tried 2, and 91, and 6, checking each one against the chart on the wall. Tatum scooted her chair over and started typing numbers into his program herself, calling out guesses first, like she was testing the probability of catching him on a wrong answer. She never did.

On Saturday, Oliver's dad arrived dusty from the commute and found him waiting outside the lab with the printout. "Show me," his dad said. Oliver typed 89. "Prime," the screen said, once, and stopped. "That's it?" his dad said. "That's it," Oliver said, and tapped the keyboard again.

activity: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll
knowledge_domain: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll
fact: A pick, also called a screen, is when an offensive player stands still in a defender's path so a teammate can get free.
story:
The track's infield had one cracked basketball hoop, and that was where Leo stood on Saturday morning, dribbling in the shade while Ms. Hosseini marked lines with chalk. Today was the day he finally got to run the offense. "You're the point guard now," Ms. Hosseini had told him at practice on Thursday, which meant Leo got to call the plays, and he had been so excited he'd barely slept.

The problem showed up immediately. Grey was guarding Leo in the drill, and Grey stuck to him like tape, shadowing every crossover, every hesitation step, every spin. Leo called for the ball from Katelyn, caught it at the top of the key, and tried to drive. Grey slid right with him. He tried again, the other way. Grey was still there, hand in his passing lane, breathing on his elbow. "You can't shake me," Grey said, grinning, clearly enjoying this.

Leo's whole plan for the morning was built on one premise: that quickness alone would get him free. He could see now how brittle that idea was. Grey wasn't faster than him, exactly, but Grey didn't need to be fast, because all Grey had to do was stay close. Leo slowed down, dribbling in place, and thought back to Tuesday, when he'd watched the older kids play on this same cracked court. One of them had been hounded by a defender just like this, unable to move, until a teammate had wandered over and simply planted himself in the defender's path, standing still as a lamppost. The defender had bumped into the wall of a body, the guard had sailed past, and the whole play had opened up like a door swinging wide.

"Katelyn," Leo called, waving her over from the wing. "Come stand right behind Grey." She looked puzzled but jogged over and planted her feet a step to Leo's left, directly in the path Grey would have to take. Then Leo drove left, hard, right at her. Grey tried to follow, and there was Katelyn, motionless, and Grey slammed into her and stumbled backward while Leo swept around her shoulder into the lane. "That's a pick," Katelyn said, laughing as she rolled toward the hoop behind the play. "Or a screen. My brother calls it both." Leo bounced the pass to her in stride and she laid it up off the chalk-dusted backboard and in.

"Yes!" Leo shouted, and even Grey was laughing, dusting himself off. "Okay, run it again," Grey said, crouching into his stance. "This time I'm ready for it." Leo held up one fist, the signal they'd invented right there on the spot, and started his dribble.

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms became part of Canada's Constitution when it was proclaimed on April 17, 1982.
story:
Leo spread the photocopy across the kitchen table and weighted the corners with forks. The assignment, due first period tomorrow, was to pick one right from the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and explain it in his own words, out loud, for a full minute. The trouble was that every time he read the words on the page, they slid back into their official language, like a song he could hum but not actually sing.

He called Olivia, because Olivia could talk her way through anything. "Just pick freedom of expression," she said through the phone. "That's the easy one."

"That's what Teresa is doing," Leo said. "She told me at lunch. If we both do it, Mr. Sutherland will think we copied."

"Then pick something weird. What's the poster say, exactly?"

Leo read down the page. At the bottom, in small print, sat a line he had skipped the first three times: proclaimed on April 17, 1982, as part of Canada's Constitution. He read it twice. "It says the Charter became part of the Constitution when it was proclaimed on April 17, 1982."

"Huh," said Olivia. "That's not that long ago. My parents were already alive."

Leo stared at the date. His intuition told him something was off, the same feeling he got when a math answer came out too neat. If the Charter only became part of the Constitution in 1982, what had people had before that? He flipped the photocopy over, then dug through his backpack for the booklet Mr. Sutherland had handed out in class. He found a page about the Constitution itself, older than the Charter, and the pieces began to fit together in his head like a puzzle whose picture had been hiding under the lid.

"Olivia, I think I've got it," he said. "It's like dinosaurs. Before 1982 the Charter was extinct, and then on April 17, 1982, it came alive as part of the Constitution. Okay, not exactly like dinosaurs. But the rights weren't always in there. Something had to happen to put them in."

"That's the thing you explain, then," Olivia said. "Teresa and I are doing expression, so you're safe. Say the date, it makes you sound smart."

Leo hung up and tried it out loud in the empty kitchen. "The Charter became part of Canada's Constitution when it was proclaimed on April 17, 1982," he said to the fridge, "and section seven says everyone has the right to life, liberty and security of the person, which in my own words means nobody can lock you up or hurt you just because they feel like it." He glanced at the clock. Nine o'clock. Still time.

The door opened and his mother came in with grocery bags, tired and damp from the rain. He hurried over and took the heaviest one before she could set it down. "Big homework?" she asked.

"Actually, it's kind of interesting," Leo said. "Want to hear my minute? You can time me."

She smiled, dropped onto a chair and held up her phone, thumb hovering over the timer. "Go."

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Looking at the horizon, a fixed distant point, can ease motion sickness because it helps the eyes agree with what the inner ear feels.
story:
The ferry to Biscayne National Park churned through water that the captain had called turbulent, and Austin gripped the rail inside the cabin while his stomach did slow somersaults. His family had planned this trip for months, a whole week of snorkeling and island trails, and now he was afraid he would spend it green and miserable. His little sister bounced beside him, completely fine, which somehow made it worse.

He found his classmates Abigael and Audrey on the bench by the window. Abigael was reading a postcard she'd bought at the dock shop. "Look," she said, holding it out. On the back, in looping handwriting, someone had written to a girl named Rosa: "Wish you were here. Remember the ferry? Stay on deck and watch the shoreline. The horizon fixes everything." Audrey squinted at it. "Weird thing to put on a postcard."

Austin read it twice. His mother had given him a motion sickness pill an hour ago, and it wasn't working. He stared at the card, thinking. The water was rough, and inside the cabin the seats and walls seemed to shift around him. But the postcard said the horizon, a fixed distant point, was what mattered. Maybe the problem wasn't the boat at all. Maybe it was what his eyes were doing in here, close in on a book, on a screen, on the walls that never held still.

"I'm going on deck," he announced. He walked carefully through the swaying cabin, out into the wind, and planted himself at the stern railing. The mainland shoreline stretched behind them, thin and steady, and beyond it the flat line where sky met sea. He fixed his eyes on that line and kept them there.
