The boat still rose and dropped, but after a few minutes the rolling settled in his stomach. He let out a long breath. It worked. He didn't know the rule behind it, only that looking at the horizon while his ears felt the boat move had somehow let the two agree.

Abigael and Audrey came out to find him. "You look better," Audrey said. "I look at the horizon," Austin told her. "That postcard was right. A fixed distant point." Abigael held the card up again and frowned. "There's no sender name," she said slowly. "And look at the front." Austin turned it over. The picture was of this exact ferry, this exact company, but the stamp was twenty years old. The shop had sold her a postcard somebody had written and never mailed. Somewhere a girl named Rosa had never gotten her message, and now three kids from another generation were standing on deck, using her advice.

Austin smiled anyway, and it was a complicated smile, because his stomach felt fine but the card made him think of the stranger who never received it. He took out his phone and snapped a picture of the horizon, then typed a message to his grandmother, who had stayed home with her bad hip: "Wish you were here. Watch the horizon. It fixes everything." Then he kept his eyes on the shoreline, all the way to the island.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: A null hypothesis is the statement that there is no relationship between the things being studied, which an experiment then tries to reject.
story:
Jeremy crouched beside the two tomato pots in the corner of the backyard, where last summer's erosion had carried away half the soil in a muddy river down the slope. Both pots looked equally barren this year, which was the whole problem. Kyleigh sat cross-legged on the old picnic blanket with her notebook open, tapping her pencil.

"Okay," she said. "You swear talking to them works. Your grandpa swore it worked. But we can't just say that."

"My grandpa hummed to his tomatoes every morning and they were taller than the fence," Jeremy said. He could still see him out there in the gray work shirt, humming something tuneless while the sprinkler ticked back and forth. Maybe it had been the humming. Maybe it had been the extra watering that came with standing there every morning. Jeremy had never thought to ask, and now he couldn't, and that bothered him more than he admitted.

Jethro arrived over the back fence, holding his phone with the speakers already blaring. "I brought the music. Half the internet says plants love Mozart, so we play Mozart for this one and nothing for that one, and we measure them every Saturday." He set the phone in front of the left pot with the ceremony of someone lighting a rocket.

"That's the experiment," Kyleigh agreed, "but first we have to say what 'no effect' would look like. My sister says it's called the null hypothesis." She wrote the words at the top of the page. "If the music does nothing, both plants grow about the same, and we have to throw out your grandpa's idea."

Jeremy frowned at the pots. "So the null hypothesis is just... silence wins? The plants grow the same either way?"

"Right. And the whole job of the experiment is to knock that down," Kyleigh said. "If we can't knock it down, we were wrong."

Jethro looked wounded. "You're telling me my phone has to spend six weeks losing to a plant that gets ignored on purpose."

Three Saturdays later, the left plant stood half an inch taller, which Kyleigh declared "basically nothing," and then a fourth Saturday arrived with the right plant suddenly catching up in one growth spurt, as if it had been sulking and then decided to try. Jeremy envied the tomatoes their simple lives: sun, water, one decision about whether to grow. He kept thinking about his grandfather's humming and whether the man had ever once measured anything, or whether he had just liked the company of the plants in the morning quiet.

"Verdict?" Jethro asked, phone in hand, Mozart ready.

Kyleigh studied her numbers, then the pots, then Jeremy. "Null hypothesis stands. For now."

Jeremy picked up the watering can and filled it at the spigot. "Then tomorrow we hum."

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: A mirror ball turns one spotlight into hundreds of moving spots of light because each small mirror tile reflects the beam in a slightly different direction.
story:
At 7:14 p.m., Theodore stood against the gym wall with his phone out, typing into the family group chat: "I'm here. Nobody is dancing yet. Everyone is standing in a big circle like it's a museum."

His mom replied first, which was already a bad sign. "You look handsome! We saw the pictures from the doorstep." Then came the photo she had taken before he left, of him in his dad's old tie, which he had not known existed until 6:40. Then his grandmother typed three thumbs up and a question mark.

He put the phone in his pocket. Across the gym, Alessandro was dancing already, alone in the middle of the circle, because Alessandro had one goal tonight and it was to win the Best Dancer vote that Ms. Hughes was running at the punch table. Alessandro had been talking about it since Tuesday. Theodore's own goal was smaller and somehow harder: stand near the dance floor for two hours without looking like a coat rack.

He moved closer, and that was when the lights went down. One spotlight clicked on above the middle of the floor, aimed up at the mirror ball, and suddenly hundreds of small spots of light swept across the gym, sliding over the bleachers, the punch table, Alessandro's elbows. Theodore frowned. One light. Hundreds of spots. He watched for a whole song, not dancing, which nobody noticed because nobody was looking at him. The spots moved together, in the same slow curve, like a school of fish. He texted the group chat: "There's one spotlight but like 500 little lights on the walls. Investigating."

His dad replied, "It's a mystery. Report back."

Theodore walked under the ball during a fast song, pretending to look for Aarav, who was at the DJ table trying to convince the DJ to let him run the last three songs. From directly below, Theodore could see the ball's surface: hundreds of small mirror tiles, each one catching the spotlight at its own angle as the ball turned. Each tile had to be throwing the beam somewhere different, because they all faced different directions. That was why the spots moved in that sweeping pattern, one tile handing the light to the next as the ball spun. He felt like a detective. A detective with no dance skills, but still.

He texted: "Solved it. The ball is covered in little mirrors, and each one reflects the beam a slightly different way. One spotlight, hundreds of moving spots. Case closed." His dad sent back a single clapping emoji. His grandmother sent the thumbs up again, plus, mysteriously, a picture of a cat.

Then Alessandro appeared beside him, sweating. "Vote for me at the punch table. I'm up against a seventh grader who can do a backflip. He's my antagonist. He intimidates people with the backflip."

"That's his whole strategy," Theodore said. It was the most logical thing anyone had said all night. He looked at the floor, where the spots were sweeping in their slow curve, and an idea assembled itself. "Follow me." He walked to the middle, waited until a patch of moving light slid toward him, and started to move with it, sweeping an arm along like the light did, stepping where the spots stepped. It looked, from a distance, like choreography. Alessandro copied him immediately, because Alessandro would copy a winning move off a lamppost. Within a minute, six kids were doing it, tracking the light across the floor.

Ms. Hughes came over with her clipboard and watched for a moment. "New dance?" she asked.

"Mirror ball style," said Alessandro.

At the punch table, the backflip kid attempted his backflip, landed on the punch table's edge, and tipped the whole bowl into the seventh grade's coats. The vote went to Alessandro by a landslide. Aarav, meanwhile, had won the DJ battle, and the last song was something slow with a horn in it. The spots swept over the gym one more time before the real lights came up, and Theodore stood in the middle of the floor, in the exact place where the light had been.

His phone buzzed. His mom, in the group chat: "Time to come home, detective."

"On my way," he typed, and pocketed the phone, still watching the last spot slide up the bleachers and out.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: In the United States, the cost of crude oil is usually the largest single part of the price of a gallon of gasoline, so pump prices tend to rise when crude oil prices rise.
story:
The price at the gas station on the corner had jumped almost forty cents since Friday, and Arianna could not stop thinking about it even with a plate of spaghetti in front of her. She had been saving babysitting money all summer for the class trip to the lake, and her mother had said the driving would cost more now. The marinara sauce smelled of garlic and basil, and the kitchen window was open, letting in the sound of the neighbor's sprinkler ticking across the lawn.

"Elias said his dad is furious," she said, twirling noodles that slid off her fork. "But I don't get it. The gas didn't change. It's still just gas."

Her father, a veteran of twenty years at the freight depot, shrugged and mopped sauce with his bread. "Prices go up, prices go down. That's how it's always been." He said it like weather, like something you persevere through rather than question.

Arianna chewed on that, and on something else. Last week she had wanted a certain hoodie, and it had been cheap because the store had racks and racks of them. Her friend Evelynn wanted a different one, sold out everywhere, and the one remaining at the vintage shop cost three times as much. Everybody wanted it, there wasn't much of it, so it was expensive. Maybe gas worked like that too, except gas came from something before it was gas. "So what's gas made from?" she asked.

"Crude oil," her mother said, passing the salad. "They refine it into gasoline."

Arianna put down her fork. In the United States, she remembered from a news segment she'd half-watched while doing homework, crude oil is usually the largest single part of the price of a gallon of gasoline. So if crude oil got more expensive, pump prices would probably rise, even though nothing at the station itself had changed. The cause was hidden, upstream, far from the pump. She pushed her glass of water away and pulled her phone from her pocket, scrolling with a vigorous thumb. "Crude oil prices went up last week. Look."

Her father leaned over, bread halfway to his mouth. "Huh. So that's it."

"Maybe," Arianna said. "I want to check. If crude oil drops next month, the pump price should drop too, right?" She wrote the station's price and today's date on the back of her hand with a pen, next to a smear of sauce. Then she took a long drink of water and looked at her mother.

"Thirty dollars extra for the trip," her mother said quietly. "We'll figure it out, or we won't."

Arianna looked at the price written on her hand and then out the window toward the corner station, its tall sign glowing white in the dusk. "Two more weekends of babysitting," she said.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: You may never divide both sides of an equation by zero, because division by zero has no answer.
story:
Victor sat on the stool by the window at the corner store, his math book open beside the slurpee machine. The owner had told him he could do homework there as long as he bought something, so a bag of chips sat sweating on the counter. The store smelled like newsprint and oranges. His worksheet wanted him to solve x + 7 = 15, and he kept getting answers that didn't check out.

Tabitha came in for a chocolate bar and stopped at his elbow. "You're doing it wrong," she said. "You're only taking the seven off one side."

"You have to take it off somewhere?" Victor said. This irritated him, because he had copied the method straight off the board.

Tabitha turned his notebook toward herself. "Think of it like a scale. A symmetrical one, arms the same length, weights in both pans. Whatever you do to one pan, you do to the other, or the whole thing tips." She wrote under his work: subtract 7, then subtract 7 again, on the other side of the equals sign. x + 7 - 7 = 15 - 7. "Now it's balanced and the x is alone."

Victor tried it on 3x = 12 and divided both sides by 3. Then he tried 4x - 2 = 10 and got it in two moves, and the answers actually worked when he plugged them back in. "Okay," he said. "Same operation, both sides. Got it."

"Want to see something rotten?" Tabitha pulled the wrapper off her chocolate bar. She wrote out a string of steps that started with a = b, multiplied both sides by a, subtracted b squared from both sides, factored, divided, and landed on 1 = 2. "Mr. Qureshi gave us this in math club. Somebody proved one equals two."

Victor read it line by line, checking each move against the rule Tabitha had just shown him. Multiplying both sides, fine. Subtracting from both sides, fine. Then he found the step where she had divided by a - b, and he went back to the top and worked out what a - b had to be. "You divided by zero," he said. "If a equals b, then a minus b is zero. That's the trick."

Tabitha snapped her chocolate bar in half and held out a piece. "So what's the rule, then?"

"You never divide both sides by zero, because division by zero has no answer." Victor took the piece. Behind them, the afternoon sun hit the glass jar of gumballs and threw a small prism of colour across his worksheet, right over the false proof.

"Cross it out," Tabitha said, and he did, pressing hard enough to tear the page.

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: At the Scripps National Spelling Bee, spellers may ask for a word's definition, part of speech, language of origin, or a sentence using it.
story:
The microphone on the auditorium stage had a small dent near the top, and Savannah stared at it while the pronouncer shuffled his cards. Three spellers were left, and the word on her card next was the only thing between her and the trophy shelf in the library, where her school kept the names of past champions. Her grandmother's name was on that shelf, spelled out in gold letters from 1982.

"Felicitous," the pronouncer said.

Savannah's mind went blank in a way that felt like a small, silent rebellion against all her weeks of studying. She knew felicity. She knew congratulate. But the ending could be spelled with an o or an e, or maybe something worse, and she could not picture the word on any page she had ever read. Beside the stage, Emile and Faisal sat in the front row, leaning forward like the word was a puzzle they could solve for her if they stared hard enough.

Then she remembered something she had overheard at regionals, two older spellers whispering in the hallway about a girl who asked questions before spelling. Not because she was stalling, one of them said, but because the answers actually helped. Savannah had wondered about that ever since. How could hearing more about a word you did not know make it easier to spell? It was like being handed a flashlight in a dark room instead of directions to the door.

"Can I have the definition?" she asked.

The pronouncer nodded. "Well chosen or apt; pleasing."

"Part of speech?" She was testing the hallway theory now, one small piece at a time, and she noticed her nerves settling as the questions came out, as if the microphone were suddenly a conversation instead of a trial.

"Adjective."

"And the language of origin?" This was the question the hallway spellers had said mattered most, though they never explained why. The pronouncer checked his card and said, "Latin." Something shifted in her mind. Latin words ending in that sound almost always took the o-u-s, like generous, like miraculous, like the curious that Mr. Becker had written on her last English paper in red pen. She had a rule now, a pattern with edges she could feel. "Could I have it in a sentence?" she asked, just to buy one more second of certainty, and the pronouncer said, "The teacher made a felicitous joke about the fire drill." Emille's mouthed wow from the front row nearly eroded her concentration, but she held on.

"Felicitous. F-E-L-I-C-I-T-O-U-S. Felicitous."

The pronouncer paused, and the pause felt long enough to make even the ceiling fans seem pessimistic. Then he said, "Correct," and the auditorium broke into applause while Faisal stood up so fast his chair banged the floor. Savannah stepped back to her mark, and the pronouncer lifted his stack of cards again. "Savannah, your next word is requiescat." She raised her hand toward the microphone. "Language of origin?"

activity: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
knowledge_domain: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
fact: A heading is a block element that stretches across the full width of its container, which is why text-align: center puts its text in the middle of the page.
story:
Thomas had been promising his grandfather all summer that he would build a web page for the old monarchy coin collection in the parlour cabinet, and all summer the coin collection had waited, unimpressed. Now, with two weeks of holiday left, Thomas sat at the wobbly kitchen table with his laptop open and a single line of HTML glaring back at him.

"The heading won't centre," he announced to the room.

His friend Mehtab, sprawled on the couch with a biscuit, looked over. "You typed centre?"

"It's spelled center in code," Thomas said. "I checked twice. It's in there, it just does nothing." The words sat stubbornly against the left edge of the page like a cat refusing to be moved.

Mehtab came over and squinted at the screen. "So where is the middle, even? Like, middle of what?"

Thomas opened a new file and typed a border around the heading, something Mr. Iyer from next door had shown him the week before. When the page refreshed, a thin rectangle appeared, and Thomas sat back so fast he nearly knocked over his tea. "Look at that. The box goes all the way across. The whole page, edge to edge." The heading wasn't just the words; it was a giant invisible slab. He pointed at the middle of the rectangle. "So the text-align thing centers the words inside the box. And the box already stretches across the full width of the page, so the words end up dead center of everything." He deleted the border, saved, and refreshed. The heading slid neatly to the middle of the screen, and Thomas punched the air.

"You discovered that with a border," Mehtab said. "Like a detective."

"Like a genius detective," said Thomas. "Write that down. No wait, don't, I'll write it down."

The door creaked and Mr. Iyer appeared with a plate of mangoes, peering at the screen. "Ah, the coin page. My granddaughter will want to see this."

"She will," Thomas said, with dignity. He turned the laptop so the centred heading faced them all, then added below it a smaller line: The Greatest Coins of the Monarchy, Probably. "Explicitly," he said, tapping the word, "in case anyone doubts it."

Mehtab reached over the laptop and typed one more word after Probably, so it read Probably Not, and Thomas tackled him off the kitchen chair while Mr. Iyer rescued the mangoes and the laptop at the same time. From the floor, Thomas called out, "I'm keeping the border on the next one. Invisible boxes, never again."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Grief can affect the body as well as feelings, often causing tiredness, trouble sleeping or changes in appetite.
story:
Edouard sat in the back seat of the family car with his tie knotted too tight, watching the cemetery gates shrink in the mirror as his father drove. Three nights since Grand-père's funeral, and three nights of lying awake until the ceiling turned grey with morning. At breakfast he had managed half a piece of toast, then hidden the rest under a napkin, the way he used to conceal vegetables under his mashed potatoes when he was small. Nobody had noticed today either, which was part of what worried him.

"You're quiet back there," his father said, taking the long way home past the river, the way Grand-père always liked.

"I think I'm getting sick," Edouard said. It came out smaller than he meant it to. "I can't sleep. And food tastes like cardboard. Maybe I caught something at the hospital, back when we visited him."

His father slowed at the light by the boat dock. "Any fever? Cough?"

"No. Just tired all day and awake all night. And I'm not hungry, like, at all."

In the seat beside him, Oceanne had ridden along to the funeral because her own family had known Grand-père from the chess club. She turned around from the front, her black headband pushed crooked from the wind. "My cousin said the same thing happened to her when our uncle died," she said. "She couldn't sleep for a whole week and her mum took her to the doctor, and the doctor said there was nothing wrong with her body. Grief can do that. It gets into your sleep and your appetite, not just your feelings."

Edouard turned that over while the bridge cables hummed past the windows. It was a strange idea, that something invisible could knock his body sideways. But if it was true, it should follow a pattern. He decided to test it the only way he could. "Okay," he said. "Tonight I try eating a real dinner even if it tastes like nothing. If I keep getting worse after that, I'll tell you I need the doctor. Deal?"

"Deal," his father said.

That evening, after dropping Oceanne at her building, they stopped at the diner where Grand-père had always ordered the onion soup. Edouard ate two bowls. It still tasted mostly of salt, but by the second one, a little of the flavour came back, and that night, for the first time since the funeral, he slept six hours straight and woke without the heavy, dragged-down feeling. He wasn't sick. He was just carrying something, and carrying it, apparently, was tiring.

At school on Monday, Koen asked how he was doing, and instead of saying fine, Edouard told him the truth, because Koen's own grandmother had been ill for a long time and would understand in the way Oceanne had. That, Edouard thought, was the one good thing about going through it: knowing what it felt like made empathy come easy.

A week later his father pulled the car into the same diner lot after chess practice. "Onion soup?" he asked, already cutting the engine.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: In the United States, a permanent change of address filed with the Postal Service forwards First-Class Mail to the new address for 12 months.
story:
Hudson stood in the middle of the empty living room, his sneakers squeaking on hardwood that no one had walked on yet. The moving truck was due tomorrow, but his mom had let him ride over with the neighbors today just so he could see the house. It smelled like fresh paint and dust, and every footstep echoed like the place was mocking him.

He had left a note in Louie's mailbox before they drove out of town. "Write to me," it said, with the new address printed in his neatest handwriting. Louie was terrible at mailing things, though. Last summer Louie had won a contest and never claimed the prize because he lost the letter. So Hudson sat on the floor of the empty room and reasoned it out. Even if Louie finally mailed something late, even months late, would it still arrive? He remembered his dad filling out a form online the night they signed the lease, something about the Postal Service forwarding mail after you file a permanent change of address. He couldn't remember the details, and that bugged him all afternoon.

A key scraped in the front door and Ms. Sharma from next door poked her head in. She was holding a plate of cookies and a roll of masking tape. "Your mother said you'd be moping in here," she said. "I brought reinforcements. Also, could you help me? I want to tape down where my furniture will go, but I can't visualize a room without seeing someone stand in it first. You're exactly the height of my couch."

Hudson got up. For twenty minutes he stood where she pointed, arms out like a shelf, while she unrolled tape on her own bare floor next door. She talked the whole time about her tulip bulbs, how she'd dug them up from her old garden and couldn't wait to get them in the ground before frost. "You look like a boy with a math problem in his head," she said finally. "Or a grudge."

"Not a grudge," Hudson said. "A question." He told her about the form his dad had filed, and about Louie. She bit a cookie and said, "You could just find out." That was annoying and also obviously right.

That evening he borrowed his mom's phone and looked it up himself. He read the page twice. Forwarding to a permanent change of address lasted twelve months for First-Class Mail. Twelve months. That was a whole year of Louie being slow and random and still getting through. Hudson felt something loosen in his chest, a tight knot of resentment at the whole move dissolving just a little.

Six weeks later, school in the new town was tolerable, and a kid named Roland had started saving him a seat at lunch. Then one Tuesday the mail carrier handed him an envelope with a crooked address on it. Inside was a drawing of two stick figures on a dock, and one line: "You still owe me a rematch in fishing." Hudson laughed out loud on the porch, then ran inside to find a pen.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: In a fair test, every other condition is kept the same, so any difference in results can be traced to the one variable that was changed.
story:
Hailey had claimed the corner of the gymnasium by the climbing ropes, where nobody practiced free throws at her head. Her project was two model catapults made of popsicle sticks, and her hypothesis, written on an index card in her best handwriting, was that a thicker rubber band would launch a marshmallow farther.

She fired the first marshmallow. It sailed past Laith, who was arranging his own project on the bleachers, and landed somewhere near the volleyball line. "Eleven tiles," Elyane called, crouching by the floor with a measuring tape. Hailey switched to the thick band on the same catapult and fired again. Four tiles. She frowned, fired again. Six.

"Your hypothesis is losing," Elyane observed.

"It's not losing, it's just not supported yet." Hailey looked from one marshmallow to the other, then at the catapults, then at the windows along the far wall. The gym had two banks of them, and her corner sat half in sun and half in shadow. She picked up both catapults and set them side by side on the same tile. "New rule. Everything stays exactly the same except the band. Same catapult arm, same angle, same spot. That way, if the results differ, the band is the only thing that could be doing it."

Laith wandered over, chewing a marshmallow that had not been fired, which Hailey noted was probably a separate problem. "Kind of like my plant project last year," he said. "One pot was by the window and one was in the hall, and Ms. Littlechild asked how I knew the water did it. I didn't. Nobody could tell what caused what."

"It's a fair test," Hailey said. "You keep every other condition the same, so any difference in the results traces back to the one variable you changed." She said it mostly to the catapults, who seemed to appreciate the clarity.

She fired ten shots with each band, alternating so the sun couldn't sneak into the data, and made Elyane categorize the marshmallows by landing zone so they could count. The thin band won eight times out of ten. The thick band stretched less and snapped harder, but slower, like a robust old door hinge. Hailey wrote "adaptation for gym conditions: shoot away from the rope pile" on a sticky note and slapped it on her poster board.

Ms. Littlechild crossed the gym, looked at the tape, the tiles, the two piles of classified marshmallows, and raised an eyebrow at Laith, who was already hiding the evidence in his mouth.

"Want to run one more trial?" Hailey asked, loading the thin band. "Elyane's got the tape. Laith's got the cleanup."

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: In parts of North America, blacklegged ticks, also called deer ticks, can spread Lyme disease, so campers there check their skin and hair for ticks after hiking through woods or tall grass.
story:
Ruby had been at Camp Wawasee for exactly one day, and she had already learned three things: the lake was colder than it looked, the oatmeal had the texture of paste, and nobody in Cabin 4 wanted to do the nightly tick check.

"It's a waste of time," Lyna said on the second night, flopping onto her bunk while the rest of them lined up by the light. "I didn't even go in the woods today."

"We went through the tall grass by the archery range," Ruby said. "You were complaining about it the whole way."

Lyna elaborated on her position, which mostly involved the words "drama" and "paranoid" and the claim that ticks were a problem for hikers, not people who stood still and missed the target. Ruby didn't argue. Instead she made her objective for the next day quiet and specific: find out whether Lyna was right, or whether the grass by the archery range was exactly the kind of place the camp was worried about.

The answer came sooner than she expected. Mr. Gagnon ran the range, and during a break he checked his own socks, plucked something off his boot, and dropped it into a jar he kept on the bench for that purpose. Ruby watched him do it. She watched the next class tramp through the same path. That evening she positioned herself in front of the cabin door with a flashlight and what she hoped was a systematic manner.

"Tick check," she said. "Everyone. Including people who didn't hike."

"You're not the boss," Lyna said, but Hana was already lifting her hair off her neck, and the other girls followed, because it was easier than arguing with someone holding a flashlight.

Ruby went last, sweeping the beam over her own arms in the mirror. It was Lyna, in the end, who found one, tiny and dark, just below the strap line of her sandal, because Lyna had bent down to prove there was nothing to find. There was a certain amount of shrieking. Hana used the tweezers from the first aid kit with the calm of someone who had an older sister.

Mr. Gagnon identified it at the infirmary. "Blacklegged tick," he said. "Some people call them deer ticks. In this part of the country they can spread Lyme disease, so we do the checks." He logged it, gave Lyna a marker circle around the spot on her ankle, and told her to keep an eye on it.

Back at the cabin, Lyna stood in the doorway with her arms crossed. "I'm doing the check tomorrow," she announced, as if it had been her idea all along.

"Great," Ruby said, and turned off the flashlight.

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: In the Northern Hemisphere, the two stars at the outer edge of the Big Dipper's bowl, called the pointer stars, point toward Polaris, the North Star.
story:
Brielle had never slept anywhere but her own bed, so the first night at Camp Wren she lay awake listening to forty strangers breathing. Around midnight, Francois whispered across the cabin, "I dare everyone to sneak to the dock." Nobody moved except Bilal, who said his phone battery was dead anyway, which made the whole dare sound pointless. Brielle sat up. If she didn't go now, she'd spend two full weeks being the girl who stayed in bed.

The dock boards were still warm from the day. Out over the lake, the sky had no streetlights in it, nothing at all, and the stars came down close enough to touch. "Bet you can't find north without a phone," Francois said, holding up his dead one. "This thing is obsolete until the charger in the lodge."

"That's not even a fair bet," Bilal said. "Nobody can find north out here."

Brielle found she was annoyed enough to contradict him. "Somebody found it before phones existed. Sailors did it all the time. They weren't guessing." She didn't know how they did it, exactly, but she remembered a piece of something, a shape with a name like kitchen equipment. She scanned the sky until she picked out seven stars in a rough spoon shape, brighter than the ones around them.

"Is that the Big Dipper?" she asked.

"Looks like a dipper to me," Francois said.

Brielle stared at it, trying to remember the rest of the half-lesson. Something about the bowl of the spoon. The two stars at the outer edge of the bowl. She traced them with her finger, then stretched the line outward, five times farther, the way the half-memory told her, and landed on a single lone star with nothing else near it.

She tested her idea instead of just believing it. "Watch that bright one, the one sitting alone," she told them, and she faced it straight on. Then she turned her back on it and pointed at where the cabins were. "The mess hall is that way, right? I ate dinner there two hours ago." Bilal confirmed it, and Francois, squinting, confirmed it too, since the hall's porch light glowed faintly behind the trees. If the lone star sat opposite the buildings they knew, then that star had to mark the direction of north. Her idea hadn't contradicted anything she could check, and one thing she could check had backed it up.

"Those two at the edge of the bowl," she said slowly, "I bet they're called the pointer stars."

"Civilians like us would never have figured that out," Francois said, lying back on the boards.

"Well, this civilian just did," Brielle said, and she lay back too, the boards warm under her shoulders, the lone star holding steady above the black water.

activity: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
knowledge_domain: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
fact: In the most basic twelve-bar blues, the band stays on the I chord for the first four bars and moves to the IV chord in bar five.
story:
Louis counted under his breath, "one, two, three, four," while Madalyn's guitar chugged out the chords and Elodie kept time on an old paint bucket with two drumsticks. Mr. Oliveira's garage smelled like sawdust and motor oil, and the space heater in the corner rattled like a second percussionist. It was Louis's turn to solo, and his hands were sweating against the neck of the borrowed guitar.

He started strong. The first four bars felt good, his fingers finding the blues scale the way Mr. Oliveira had shown him, bending the third note until it almost cried. Then, somewhere in bar four, Louis heard the band change beneath him and jumped to a new cluster of notes to match it. The clash was instant and ugly, like two people saying different words at the same time. Elodie winced. Madalyn kept playing, but her eyebrows went up.

"Wait," Louis said, holding up a hand. He stopped and stared at the garage floor, thinking of the recital at school last spring. His older cousin had soloed there, and Louis had watched her band stay on one chord for what felt like forever before finally shifting. He had assumed the shift happened whenever the soloist felt it, like a conversation. Now he wondered if the change came at a fixed spot instead, and if his job was only to notice where the spot was.

"Let me try an analysis," he said, mostly to himself. "Play the chords again, no solo." Madalyn played. Louis tapped his knee on every bar and said the numbers out loud. One, two, three, four on the same chord, then a change exactly on bar five, then back, then the shift near the end. It was proportional, like a recipe: four parts of the first chord before anything moved. He had been switching his notes one bar early, guessing instead of counting. The pattern was invisible, but it was there, and it was regular.

"From the top," he said. This time he counted silently, one, two, three, four, and let his notes flourish over the same chord, waiting. When bar five arrived and the band shifted, he shifted with it, and the notes locked together like gears. Elodie whooped without dropping a beat. It was the best sixteen bars of his life, and then it was over, because Madalyn's amplifier crackled and died, and the recital was tomorrow. Louis unplugged it, turned it over, and peered at the tangled cord inside.

"Anybody got a screwdriver?"

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: A control group is treated exactly like the test group except for the one thing being tested, so any difference can be traced to that change.
story:
Maya lined the six bean plants along her bedroom windowsill, each one in a paper cup with a number painted on the side. For her science project she had mixed a powder her uncle swore by into the soil of every cup, and in two weeks the plants had shot up so fast she could almost watch them grow. "See?" her dad said, leaning in the doorway. "That stuff is influential. Best fertilizer on the shelf." Maya nodded, but a small itch started at the back of her mind. How would she prove the fertilizer was doing it, and not the sunny window or her careful watering?

She called Rehan, who was doing the same project for Ms. Villanueva's class. "What did you do for yours?" she asked. "Fertilizer," he said. "All my plants got it, and they're huge." Maya chewed the end of her pencil. So Rehan had the same results and the same problem. If everything got the powder, what could they compare it to? She inferred that the fertilizer might be the cause, but inferring wasn't the same as showing. "Try something for me," she said. "Tomorrow, scoop the fertilizer into every other cup, not all of them. Same soil, same water, same spot."

The next afternoon Rehan sent a photo of his tray, and Maya set up hers the same way. Cups one, three, and five kept the fertilizer. Cups two, four, and six got plain soil, and she watered all six with the same measuring cup, in the same order, at the same time. "They're treated exactly alike," she told Rehan on the porch, "except for the one thing we're testing." Rehan tilted his head. "Ms. Villanueva would call those untreated ones a control group," he said. Maya wrote the words in her notebook and underlined them twice.

For ten days she measured every stem with a ruler and logged the numbers in a table. The fertilized plants stayed ahead, but only by a little, and cup four, one of the plain ones, grew tallest of all. Maya frowned at the page. Could the fertilizer really be the cause? She checked the light. Cup four sat at the sunny end of the sill, where the morning came in strongest, and she realized she had to move the cups around each day so every plant spent equal time there. The window was part of the little ecosystem on her sill, and light was doing its own quiet work.

When the growing stopped, she spread her table on the kitchen table for her dad. Same soil, same water, same light, she said, and only one difference between the two groups. The fertilized plants were taller by four centimeters on average. "So the powder helped," her dad said. "A little," Maya said. "Not like the ad says." She looked at the numbers again and wondered what else she could test. Could too much fertilizer hurt? What would happen with half the dose?

At school, Ms. Villanueva circled Maya's control group column in green pen and wrote one word at the top. Maya leaned closer to read it. "At last," the note said.

activity: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark
knowledge_domain: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark
fact: In traditional transparent watercolour, the brightest highlights, like the shine in an eye, are usually made by leaving the white paper unpainted rather than adding white paint.
story:
The portrait was supposed to be of Troy, and so far it looked like a potato with excellent hair. Vincent sat cross-legged in the backyard with his watercolour block propped on a clipboard, Troy slumped on a lawn chair across from him, and Levi eating crackers on the picnic blanket like he was at a gallery opening. "Hold still," Vincent said. "You're ruining the light."

"The light is ruining me," Troy said. "I'm getting fatigue from posing. That's a real thing. Look it up."

"It is not." Vincent dipped his brush and laid a pale wash of yellow over Troy's whole face, the way Ms. Kelly had shown the summer camp class on Monday: lightest colours first, then darker layers on top. He was proud of that first wash. It was even. It was smooth. It covered absolutely everything, including both of Troy's eyes, which was a detail that would not matter for another twenty minutes.

Levi leaned over his shoulder while the wash dried. "You should allocate some crackers to the artist," he announced. "Great art requires snacks." He held out the box, then squinted at the paper. "Wait. Where's the gleam in his eye?"

"The what?"

"The little white shine. Every portrait has it. My grandma's has like four."

Vincent looked at his painting, then at Troy's actual eyes, which had a small bright spot in each where the sun caught them. He reached for his white paint, then stopped, because he remembered something Ms. Kelly had said at camp while walking past another kid's easel: "The brightest highlights are the paper itself. You leave those spots bare." He had been half-listening at the time, which now seemed like a bizarre way to treat useful information. He had painted over both eye spots completely.

"So fix it with white paint," Troy said.

"It doesn't work like that. If white paint worked, I'd have used white paint." Vincent tapped the brush against his chin. The idea felt strange, but he could test it. He had a scrap of the same paper. He painted a small square with his yellow wash, let it dry, then dabbed white paint on half of it and left the other half bare. When it dried, he held it up to the light. The painted half looked chalky, not bright. The bare half glowed like a tiny window. It was actually kind of amazing. The shiniest thing in the picture was the part with nothing on it.

He started the face over, and this time, before the first wash touched the paper, he took the end of his paintbrush handle and pressed two tiny circles of masking fluid onto Troy's eyes. "That stuff keeps the paper blank where you want it," he told Levi, who was watching with a cracker halfway to his mouth. Troy held still for a whole hour after that, partly out of friendship and partly because Vincent threatened to paint him with a unibrow. When Vincent finally peeled the little rubbery dots away, there they were: two perfect sparks of white paper, shining in Troy's eyes like the sun had been captured in there. Levi stood up and clapped slowly, crumbs falling off his shirt.

"Two gleams," Troy said, admiring himself on paper. "Grandma's only got four because she's twice as old."
